      - text: Interval type

        - slider "Graph right endpoint"

      - text: Greatest value=3 at x=-1, 2 Least value=-1 at x=-2, 1
    - complementary:
      - heading "EXTREME VALUE THEOREM" [level=3]
      - paragraph: If f is continuous on a closed interval [a,b], then f attains an absolute maximum and minimum.
      - heading "CLOSED-INTERVAL METHOD" [level=3]
      - list:
        - listitem: Find critical points inside (a,b).
        - listitem: Evaluate f at critical points and included endpoints.
        - listitem: Compare all candidate values.
      - heading "IMPORTANT WARNING" [level=3]
      - paragraph: Do not assume local extrema are absolute. Always check endpoints.
      - heading "WORKED EXAMPLE" [level=3]
      - paragraph: On [−2,2], candidates are −2,−1,1,2.
      - table:
        - rowgroup:
          - row "-2 -1":
            - cell "-2"
            - cell "-1"
          - row "-1 3":
            - cell "-1"
            - cell "3"
          - row "1 -1":
            - cell "1"
            - cell "-1"
          - row "2 3":
            - cell "2"
            - cell "3"
      - text: Absolute maximum=3 at x=−1,2. Absolute minimum=−1 at x=−2,1.
    - article:
      - heading "HOW INTERVAL TYPE AFFECTS EXTREMA" [level=3]
      - paragraph: Closed intervals include endpoints and invoke the Extreme Value Theorem. Open intervals exclude endpoints; extrema may or may not still be attained at interior critical points.
    - article:
      - text: Closed interval
      - paragraph: Endpoints included; extrema guaranteed for continuous f.
    - article:
      - text: Open interval
      - paragraph: Endpoints excluded; inspect interior critical points and limiting behavior.
